newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's leader, Jordan's king meet in secret.
newsitem.headline: Israel's leader, Jordan's king meet in secret.

text.p: Israel and Jordan said on Friday their leaders had met secretly at a Jordanian resort for several hours late at night to begin patching up a water dispute and to try to salvage Middle East peacemaking.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Jordan's King Hussein met at the Red Sea port of Aqaba, officials said. They confirmed the Thursday night meeting after news of it leaked to Israel's biggest newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth.

"I believe we also found solutions and I want to emphasise there was no concession on Israel's part," said Ariel Sharon, who attended the meeting as Israel's national infrastructure minister responsible for water.
Yedioth Ahronoth said the Israelis flew in military helicopters to the summit.

It was the first time the king had met Sharon, a former general, who told Israel Radio: "To my regret my meetings in the past with the Kingdom of Jordan were in different circumstances of war and fighting."
It was unclear why the summit between two countries at peace for nearly three years took place in secret. But the last planned public meeting, on Tuesday, was cancelled.
Jordan's Crown Prince Hassan cancelled the meeting with Netanyahu because of disagreements over water supplies Israel promised the parched Arab kingdom under their 1994 peace treaty.

Jordan might also have sought to keep the meeting quiet rather than give Netanyahu a public relations prize at a time when Palestinian talks with Israel are in crisis over construction of a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
In Jerusalem and the Palestinian-ruled Gaza Strip, U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross appeared to make little headway in his mission to save Israeli-Palestinian negotiations.

Jordan's Information Minister Samir Mutawae confirmed to Reuters that the king had hosted Netanyahu. An Israeli cabinet statement said professionals on both sides would go on working toward a solution of the water dispute.
Jordanian officials had accused Israel of backing out at the last minute from an accord to help Jordan find an extra 50 million cubic metres of water a year.
Their treaty, ending a 46-year state of war, specified that within a year of its coming into force in November 1994 the two sides would develop a plan to supply Jordan with the water.
Ideas for the water supply included desalination plants, dam building, and steps to ease pollution of river waters. But no plan was formally implemented.

Jordanian Foreign Minister Fayez al-Tarawneh spoke this week of a "frustration in the whole peace process" among Jordanians, and said Israel's failure to follow up its commitment to help find water supplies for Jordan was a breach of the 1994 treaty.

Peace talks between Israel and the Palestinians broke down two months ago after Netanyahu gave the final go-ahead for the construction of 6,500 houses for Jews in Arab East Jerusalem on land occupied by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.
Mutawae said: "The developments in the peace process and the obstacles facing it were discussed and the necessity of pushing them ahead, especially on the Palestinian-Israeli track."
